name: a letter asking for what its writer cannot know
one_line: A letter from one person to one person, which knows something the reader does not, and asks in return for something its writer could not possibly know.
how: Write it as a letter and not as a task: no heading, no instructions, a first name or a single initial at the foot, and a small reason for writing. Give the writer one thing the reader has not got — a mark that used to be on a wall, a method that does not work, a count they cannot settle — and do not explain it. Ask for little, and say so: «even three lines», with five ruled lines underneath saying the same thing without words. Then the request that pays for the page: something the writer could not know — a thing that happened after they left, a case where their method fails. Somewhere put one line saying who found this letter and put it on the table, because there is no postman and pretending otherwise is a lie the reader will find.

knobs.effect: Somebody who knows something and withholds it produces a question worth answering. Somebody who needs something they cannot do produces a task with a reason. Authority produces neither: an office that orders is a module.
A letter that expects one and gets none is a small betrayal. Naming whoever found the letter and put it there costs one line, keeps the asymmetry and promises no postman.
«Even three lines» with five printed rules gets three lines written. A blank half page asks for an essay and comes back empty, and it was the letter that set that, not the reader.
Nothing explained is a letter, and the gaps are what there is to answer. Everything explained is a briefing with a signature at the bottom, and there is nothing left to reconstruct.

where_the_work_is: In the last request. Everything else on the page could be answered by anybody; the line asking for what the writer cannot know makes the reader the only possible source, which is the reverse of a school question.
breaks: There is no sender, so the reply goes nowhere; the honest repair is naming whoever put the letter on the table, and it costs half the effect. On 800x480 a letter cannot be read at all — it is prose, and prose in one bit at that size is four sentences. A display can say one has arrived; the letter has to be paper, folded, in a hand.
